The Severity/Priority levels reported by Customer will be determined by Procore in its reasonable discretion, taking into consideration Customer’s report of the impact and functionality of the issue and impact to Customer. Once Procore receives an error ticket as reported from Customer, Procore shall provide Customer with timely status updates as reasonably determined by Procore until a workaround or other resolution is established by Procore. 134 Agenda Staff Report TO: Mayor Amabile and City Council Members FROM: Soknirorn Than, City Manager DATE: September 16, 2026 TYPE OF REPORT: Consent Item SUBJECT: Approval of an Amendment with Mid Valley IT to Upgrade City Hall Server Recommendation: It is recommended that the City Council adopts the Resolution approving an amendment to the agreement with Mid Valley IT to upgrade City Hall Server in the amount of $335,344.35 and authorizing the City Manager to execute the amendment including the contingency of 10% in the amount of $33,534.00. Background: The City of Los Banos currently contracts for managed IT services to support daily operations, cybersecurity, infrastructure maintenance, and technology planning. The City issued a request for updated service proposals to ensure continuity of service and compliance with new operational and legislative requirements, including SB 707. Mid Valley IT has provided a comprehensive proposal for a fixed monthly managed services agreement, along with additional audio/visual upgrades required for SB 707 compliance. On March 18, 2026, the City Council approved a Managed IT Services Agreement with Mid Valley IT effective April 1, 2026, for a three-year term. Under the agreement, Mid Valley IT provides comprehensive managed information technology services, including unlimited remote and on-site technical support, regular onsite visits, network documentation, capital planning assistance, antivirus hosting and monitoring, a standard 48-hour response time for service requests, and a four-hour response time for emergency issues.
135 ITEM 7H The agreement establishes a fixed monthly service fee of $12,877, subject to a 3.5% annual cost-of-living adjustment. In addition to the base support services, the City may utilize optional subscription-based technology services, including endpoint detection and response (EDR) antivirus protection, Duo multi-factor authentication, Inky email filtering, Microsoft 365 licensing at published Microsoft rates, and managed backup services currently billed at $2,380 per month. The agreement was intended to provide predictable IT support costs and ensure ongoing maintenance, cybersecurity monitoring, technology planning, and operational support for the City's information technology infrastructure. Discussion: The City Hall server infrastructure is a critical component of the City's information technology environment, supporting daily operations, data storage, business applications, cybersecurity functions, and interdepartmental communications. Much of the City's existing server and storage environment has reached the point where replacement and modernization are necessary to maintain system reliability, improve performance, and support future technology needs. The proposed project would replace the current server cluster and storage platform with a modern, centralized infrastructure consisting of new Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) servers, a Storage Area Network (SAN), high-speed network switching equipment, and an upgraded backup environment. The project also includes migration of existing virtual servers, implementation of a clustered server architecture, and upgrades of approximately 18 virtual machines to Windows Server 2025. A key benefit of the proposed upgrade is the establishment of a centralized management platform for both network and storage resources. Centralized administration will allow Information Technology staff and the City's managed service provider to more efficiently monitor system health, manage security updates, allocate storage resources, and respond to operational issues. The upgraded environment will improve scalability, simplify maintenance activities, and reduce the risk associated with aging hardware and fragmented storage systems. This centralized approach allows for a unified system to branch facilities such as the new Development Services Center (at the old PD Annex Building), and the Fire Station No. 4. This will lower cost for firewall and subscriptions. The project also enhances the City's cybersecurity and disaster recovery capabilities. The addition of a dedicated backup appliance, modern storage architecture, and updated server operating systems will strengthen data protection, improve system resiliency, and support business continuity in the event of equipment failure, cybersecurity incidents, or other service disruptions. The proposed solution includes two enterprise-grade HPE data center switches, an HPE MSA 2070 SAN with high-performance solid-state storage, four new HPE ProLiant Gen12 servers configured in a clustered environment, Windows Server 2025 licensing, and 136 associated implementation services. Mid Valley IT will provide professional services to design, install, configure, and migrate the City's virtual server environment to the new platform. The total project cost is $335,344.35 including equipment, software licensing, labor, sales tax, and installation services. Staff is requesting a 10% contingency in the amount of $33,534.00 to allow for unforeseen conditions associated with this upgrade. Staff believes the proposed investment is necessary to ensure the continued reliability, security, and performance of the City's core technology infrastructure while providing a scalable platform capable of supporting future service delivery, operational efficiency, and technology modernization initiatives. Procurement: Pursuant to Los Banos Municipal Code Section 3-10.230, staff recommends utilizing noncompetitive negotiation for the procurement of the City Hall Server Cluster and Network Infrastructure Upgrade. The proposed purchase qualifies under multiple provisions of Section 3-10.230, including: 1. Technology products, including enterprise servers, storage area network (SAN) equipment, network switching infrastructure, virtualization software, and associated licensing. 2. Additions to and maintenance of existing equipment that can be more efficiently performed by a particular company with knowledge of the City's existing environment. 3. Equipment that must be compatible with existing systems, network architecture, virtualization platforms, cybersecurity controls, and operational procedures supported by the City's managed information technology services provider. Mid Valley IT currently serves as the City's managed IT services provider under a long-term support agreement and is responsible for maintaining the City's network, server infrastructure, cybersecurity systems, backups, and daily technology operations. The proposed solution was specifically designed to integrate with the City's existing environment and includes migration of approximately 18 virtual servers, implementation of centralized storage, and configuration of a new clustered server architecture. Utilizing Mid Valley IT for this project provides continuity of operations, minimizes implementation risk, reduces system downtime during migration, and ensures compatibility with the City's existing technology infrastructure. Consistent with Section 3-10.230, staff finds that the proposed procurement involves specialized technology products and system upgrades that must be integrated with existing infrastructure and supported by the City's current managed service provider. Staff further finds that the proposed procurement is in the City's best interest because it provides a complete, integrated solution that enhances reliability, cybersecurity, centralized management, and long-term operational efficiency while reducing the risks associated with transitioning critical infrastructure to an unfamiliar vendor. 137 Fiscal Impact: Funding for this upgrade is budgeted for within the Information Technology Division for Fiscal Year 2026-2027 in account 610-410-100-770 for a total amount of $400,000.00. Customer Initials 152 Agenda Staff Report TO: Mayor Amabile and City Council Members FROM: Stacy Souza Elms, Community and Economic Development Director DATE: September 16, 2026 TYPE OF REPORT: Agenda Item SUBJECT: Approval of a Professional Services Agreement with 4LEAF, Inc. for Building and Fire Prevention Services and Authorization for the City Manager to Execute the Agreement ______________________________________________________________________ Recommendation: Adopt a Resolution approving a Professional Services Agreement with 4LEAF, Inc. for Building and Fire Prevention Services and authorizing the City Manager to execute the Agreement. Background: The City released a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for Building and Fire Prevention Services on April 8, 2026, seeking a qualified consultant to provide comprehensive building and fire prevention services, including an on-call Certified Building Official, permit processing, plan review, inspections, code enforcement support, and related administrative functions. Proposals were due on May 6, 2026. The RFQ indicated that qualifications would be evaluated based on consultant experience, organizational approach, staff availability, past performance, and overall qualifications. The City received five (5) Statements of Qualifications from the following firms: 1. True North Compliance Services 2. CSG Consultants, Inc.
3. Bureau Veritas North America 4. 4LEAF, Inc.
153 ITEM 8 5. Shums Coda Associates The RFQ evaluation process was conducted in accordance with the evaluation criteria established in the solicitation documents. The City reviewed the qualifications, staffing resources, municipal experience, service delivery capabilities, and overall ability of each firm to meet the City's operational needs. The RFQ specifically emphasized staff availability, qualifications and experience, project approach, and demonstrated success providing services to public agencies. Based on the evaluation of qualifications and experience, staff determined that 4LEAF, Inc. was the most qualified firm to provide the requested services. 4LEAF demonstrated extensive experience providing contract building department services throughout California and possesses the staffing resources and technical capabilities necessary to support the City's development review and permitting activities. Staff subsequently negotiated a Professional Services Agreement with 4LEAF that reflects the service requirements identified in the RFQ and is in the best interest of the City. Discussion: Under the proposed agreement, 4LEAF will provide comprehensive building and fire prevention services including: • Certified Building Official services; • Building permit processing and administration; • Building and fire plan review services; • Building inspection services; • Building code enforcement support; • Accessibility review services; • On-call and emergency response services; and • Support for the City's electronic permitting and Tyler Technologies systems. The agreement includes performance standards and review timelines intended to ensure efficient permit processing and customer service. The consultant will provide qualified personnel with the necessary certifications and experience to maintain continuity of operations and respond to fluctuating development activity levels. Background: State legislative and regulatory actions have a significant impact on municipal operations, funding, service delivery, infrastructure development, housing, public safety, environmental compliance, and economic development. As Los Banos continues to grow, state policies increasingly influence the City's ability to address local priorities and deliver services efficiently to residents and businesses. The City has historically engaged with state legislators, regional partners, advocacy organizations, and state agencies to advance local priorities and secure funding opportunities. Adoption of an annual legislative platform provides a framework for those advocacy efforts and allows the City to respond in a timely manner to legislation and budget proposals during the legislative session. The proposed Fiscal Year 2026-27 Legislative Priorities were developed by Nossaman LLP, our state advocacy partner, based on City Council goals, General Plan objectives, adopted budget priorities, infrastructure needs, public safety objectives, and operational 179 ITEM 9 responsibilities. The platform is intended to remain broad enough to address evolving legislative issues while providing clear policy direction. Discussion: The legislative platform establishes guiding principles that enable the City to respond efficiently and consistently to emerging legislative issues while advancing Council priorities and community interests. The platform focuses on six (6) key policy areas: 1. Fiscal Stability, Local Control, and Core Services a. The platform supports preserving local control over land use, public services, infrastructure planning, and fiscal decisions that are best addressed by locally elected officials. The City advocates for the protection of locally generated revenues, adequate funding for state-mandated programs, and regulatory flexibility that allows local governments to implement state requirements in a practical and cost-effective manner. These priorities help ensure that Los Banos can continue providing essential services, including public safety, street maintenance, water and wastewater operations, parks, and community development services while maintaining long-term fiscal sustainability. 2. Water, Sustainability, and Environmental Resources a. Reliable access to safe drinking water remains one of the City's most critical responsibilities. The platform supports state investments and policies that strengthen water quality compliance, groundwater sustainability, drought resilience, recycled water development, stormwater management, and regional water supply planning. The City also supports funding and technical assistance to address emerging contaminants and environmental requirements while minimizing financial impacts on ratepayers. Additionally, the platform recognizes the importance of climate resilience, emergency preparedness, and protecting community assets from natural and environmental hazards. 3. Economic Development, Downtown, and Local Jobs a. Economic growth is essential to maintaining a healthy local economy and expanding opportunities for residents. The legislative platform supports policies and programs that promote business attraction and retention, workforce development, infrastructure readiness, small business support, and job creation. The City also seeks investment in downtown revitalization, public improvements, tourism, arts, culture, and placemaking initiatives that strengthen Downtown Los Banos as a community gathering place and economic center. These efforts support a diversified tax base and help ensure that growing inland communities receive equitable consideration in statewide economic development programs. 4. Housing, Growth, and Neighborhood Quality 180 a. Los Banos continues to experience significant growth and housing demand. The platform supports policies that encourage the development of attainable and affordable housing while recognizing the corresponding need for infrastructure, transportation improvements, public safety services, parks, and other community facilities. The City advocates for preserving local planning authority and ensuring that housing production requirements remain balanced with community character, infrastructure capacity, and neighborhood compatibility. The platform also supports practical solutions and funding opportunities related to homelessness, behavioral health services, substance abuse treatment, domestic violence prevention, and youth services. 5. Streets, Transportation, Utilities, and Public Facilities a. The City has substantial ongoing needs related to roadway maintenance, traffic safety improvements, utility infrastructure, stormwater systems, parks, public facilities, and technology investments. The legislative platform supports increased and sustainable funding sources for capital improvements, maintenance programs, and infrastructure modernization efforts. The City also seeks grant opportunities and financing tools that help fund critical projects while minimizing impacts on local taxpayers and utility ratepayers. Transportation investments that improve safety, reduce congestion, and enhance regional connectivity are particularly important to supporting future growth and economic development. 6. Public Safety and Emergency Response a. Protecting residents and businesses remains a core City responsibility. The platform supports legislation and funding that strengthen police, fire, emergency medical, and disaster response capabilities. Priority areas include maintaining emergency response times, recruiting and retaining qualified personnel, investing in equipment and facilities, enhancing emergency preparedness, and supporting crime prevention initiatives. The City also recognizes the importance of youth programs, behavioral health services, violence prevention strategies, and community-based partnerships that address root causes of crime and improve neighborhood safety. Investments in emergency operations, disaster recovery, critical infrastructure protection, and mutual aid capabilities further support the City's commitment to public safety and community resilience. Fiscal Impact: Adoption of the Legislative Priorities does not have a direct fiscal impact. However, the platform provides guidance for pursuing grant funding, advocating for state budget appropriations, influencing legislation affecting municipal finances, and seeking resources that may reduce future costs or support City infrastructure and service needs. 181 Reviewed by: _______________________________ _______________________________ Mary Lerner, City Attorney Minerva Moreno, Finance Director Attachment: 1. The project will consolidate Community and Economic Development, Building, Public Works Administration, Engineering, Fire Prevention, and related public-facing services into a centralized location designed to improve customer service, accessibility, and operational efficiency. The existing two-story building contains approximately 11,255 square feet and is located within the Downtown Mixed-Use area. The project includes interior renovations to create public service counters, customer waiting areas, meeting spaces, staff workstations, and administrative offices. Exterior improvements include modernization of the building façade, landscaping, pedestrian walkways, parking lot enhancements, public art, and a public plaza that will create a more inviting civic presence in the downtown area. The project reuses an existing public facility without expanding the building footprint and maintains the site's established circulation patterns and municipal office use. 191 ITEM 10 On September 9, 2026, the Planning Commission considered and approved Site Plan Review No. 2026-08 and determined the project to be categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15301 (Existing Facilities). Next Steps: The project team is currently completing the Schematic Design phase of the project. The approved schematic design will be further refined through construction document preparation and cost estimating as part of the City's Progressive Design-Build process. The current project schedule anticipates completion of schematic design in October 2026, followed by preparation of construction documents and development of a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP) proposal. Staff will be returning to the City Council with the final project design, project budget updates, and a GMP contract amendment for Council consideration and authorization to proceed with construction. Fiscal Impact: The Development Services Center project is funded through appropriations included in the Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget. No additional appropriation is requested as part of this informational update. Background: On December 3, 2025, the County of Merced released a Request for Proposals (RFP) No. 7646, for funding available through the State of California’s HHAP Program to support Rapid Rehousing activities. The HHAP Program provides flexible funding to cities, counties, and Continuums of Care to assist individuals experiencing homelessness and increase access to housing and supportive services. On December 22, 2025, the City of Los Banos submitted a proposal in response to the County’s RFP. On February 4, 2026, the County issued an Intent to Negotiate letter notifying the City that its proposal had been ranked the highest and selected for funding in the amount of $134,500.00. 201 ITEM 11 The funding will support Rapid Rehousing activities, including rental deposits, rental application fees, landlord engagement, and landlord incentives. While the primary focus of the funding will be to support residents housed through the One Tree Permanent Supportive Housing project, the funds may also be used to assist eligible individuals residing in other rental housing throughout the community. On August 11, 2026, the County submitted the draft agreement to the City for review. The agreement has since been reviewed by the City Attorney and Finance Director and is now presented to the City Council for approval and authorization of execution by the City Manager. Discussion: The City's Housing Division is responsible for coordinating local efforts to address homelessness. Services include outreach and engagement, case management, housing navigation, and connections to supportive services, benefits, healthcare, and housing resources. The Housing Division also actively pursues grant funding opportunities to expand housing options and services for individuals experiencing homelessness. According to County Continuum of Care 2026 Point-in-Time Count, 101 individuals experiencing homelessness were identified within the City of Los Banos. Approval of the HHAP contract will provide additional resources to remove common barriers to housing, including rental deposits and application costs. The funding will also support landlord engagement efforts and incentive programs designed to increase housing opportunities for individuals experiencing homelessness. These resources will enhance the City's ability to successfully place eligible individuals into permanent housing, including units within the One Tree Permanent Supportive Housing development. The proposed contract will provide $134,500 in grant funding to support rapid rehousing efforts and assist individuals experiencing homelessness in obtaining and maintaining permanent housing. Fiscal Impact: There is no impact to the General Fund. Acceptance of the HHAP grant will increase both revenues and expenditures by $134,500 in Fiscal Year 2026-27. Grant revenue will be recognized in Account No. 100-000-339-010 (Other Grants), with corresponding expenditures appropriated in Account No. 100-419-130-273 (Special Departmental Expense) for eligible HHAP program activities. CTI is a time-limited, evidence-based case management model designed to support individuals who are experiencing homelessness or other major life transitions. CTI focuses on providing intensive support in the early stages of a transition to ensure that individuals do not experience setbacks or crises that could derail their progress. The key components of CTI include time-limited support, strengthening social supports, collaboration with other services, gradual reduction of support, and a focus on crisis prevention. I. Employ Motivational Interviewing (MI) techniques. MI is a client-centered, collaborative counseling approach designed to help individuals explore and resolve ambivalence about behavior change. The goal is to enhance a person's intrinsic motivation to make positive changes by creating an empathetic and non-judgmental environment. MI is often used in situations where individuals may be uncertain or resistant to change, such as in addressing substance use, mental health issues, or behaviors linked to chronic conditions. The key components of MI include expressing empathy, identifying discrepancies, rolling with resistance, supporting self-efficacy, elicit change talk, and autonomy and choice. J. Employ Harm Reduction techniques. Harm Reduction is an approach aimed at minimizing the negative consequences associated with certain behaviors, particularly those that are risky or potentially harmful, such as substance use. Rather than focusing solely on eliminating the behavior (such as requiring individuals to stop using drugs or alcohol), harm reduction acknowledges that some individuals may not be ready or able to stop immediately. The key 226 21 components of Harm Reduction include a non-judgmental approach, focus on practical strategies, health and safety over abstinence, empowerment and choice, holistic and person-centered approaches, and collaboration and support. Participant Eligibility The Contractor shall determine and document each participant’s eligibility based on the following project types: 1. Rapid Re-Housing and Emergency Shelter a. Participants must meet the criteria of at least one of the following definitions: i. 24 CFR 578.3 “Homeless” under subsection (1) ii. 24 CFR 578.3 “Homeless” under subsection (4) 5. Program Outcomes The California System Performance Measures (CA SPMs) are a standardized set of metrics to help assess progress towards preventing, reducing, and ending homelessness. The Contractor shall maintain or improve the following relevant CA SPMs for the contracted program. Measure 1a: The number of people accessing services who are experiencing homelessness. 246 41 Defining Factors: This measure is evaluated in comparison with the number of individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness as identified in CA SPM 1b. Improvements: If the number of people served under CA SPM 1a increases by a rate greater than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that the program is reaching and supporting more people than before. If the number of people served under CA SPM 1a decreases by a rate that is the same or less than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that there are less services needed and that access is declining proportionally. Measure 1b: The estimated number of people experiencing unsheltered homelessness on the CoC’s Point-in-Time Count (on a single day in the last week of January). Improvement: A decrease in CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that there are less people experiencing unsheltered homelessness. Measure 2: The number of persons entering the system who are experiencing homelessness for the first time. Defining Factors: This is measured by the number of people accessing services who are experiencing homelessness for the first time (defined as not accessing services while experiencing homelessness in the past two years). This measure is evaluated in comparison with the number of individuals experiencing unsheltered homelessness as identified in CA SPM 1b. Improvements: If the number of people served under CA SPM 2 increases by a rate greater than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that the program is reaching and supporting more people than before. If the number of people served under CA SPM 2 decreases by a rate that is the same or less than the number experiencing unsheltered homelessness under CA SPM 1b. This would indicate that there are less services needed and that access is declining proportionally. Measure 3: The number of people exiting homelessness into permanent housing. 247 42 Defining Factors: This is measured by the number of people exiting homelessness into permanent housing, including people who exited the homelessness response system to permanent housing and people who moved into permanent housing within the homelessness response system. Improvement: An increase in CA SPM 3. This would indicate that there is an increase in permanent housing outcomes both inside and outside the homelessness response system. Measure 4: Length of time persons remained homeless. Defining Factors: This is measured by the average length of time (in number of days) that people were enrolled in street outreach (SO) or other non-residential projects (while experiencing homelessness), emergency shelter (ES), transitional housing (TH), and safe haven (SH) projects, as well as time during which people were enrolled in, but had not yet moved into, rapid rehousing (RRH), permanent supportive housing (PSH), and other permanent housing (OPH) projects. Improvement: A decrease in CA SPM 4. This would indicate that there is a decrease in the length of time people experience homelessness while accessing services. Measure 5: Number of persons who return to homelessness after exiting homelessness to permanent housing. Defining Factors: This is measured by the percentage of people who return to homelessness within six months of exiting the homelessness response system to permanent housing. Improvement: A decrease in CA SPM 5. This would indicate that people experiencing homelessness are being provided adequate services to maintain their permanent housing. Measure 6: Successful placements from street outreach. Defining Factors: This is measured by the number of people with successful placements from street outreach projects, which includes exits to an emergency shelter (ES), safe haven (SH), transitional housing (TH), or permanent housing (PH) destinations. Improvement: An increase in CA SPM 6. This would indicate the success of street outreach in connecting people to shelter, interim, or permanent housing solutions. 248 43 The AE shall monitor progress for the CA SPMs utilizing the System Administrator Report [HUDX-223-AD] System Performance Measures within HMIS. Each of the following CA SPMs will be analyzed for the corresponding program types. CA SPM Street Outreach Emergency Shelter Homelessness Prevention Rapid Re-Housing Measure 1a    Measure 1b    Measure 2    Measure 3   Measure 4   Measure 5   Measure 6   6. Housing First Approach The Contractor shall provide eligible activities for all programs and projects in a manner consistent with the housing first practices described in California Code of Regulations, title 25, section 8409(b)(1)-(6). Allocated funds for eligible activities that provide permanent housing shall incorporate the core components of Housing First as provided in Section 8255(b) of the Welfare and Institutions Code. The Contractor shall allow entry to program participants regardless of their income, current or past substance use, criminal records, or history of domestic violence. Programs also should not terminate clients regardless of whether or not they participate in supportive services, make progress on a service plan, lose their income, or based on other activities not covered in a lease agreement typically found for an unassisted person in the program’s geographic area. The Contractor shall assume the following responsibilities for implementing a Housing First and Low Barrier approach within their programs: 1. Policies and Procedures a. The Contractor shall develop, implement, and maintain written policies and procedures that fully detail their Housing First and Low Barrier operations for all program types. 2. Program Access: a. Admission to the program will not be contingent upon pre-requisites such as abstinence of substances, minimum income requirements, health or mental health history, medication adherence, age, criminal justice history, financial history, completion of treatment, participation in services, “housing readiness”, history or occurrence of victimization, survivor of sexual assault or an affiliated person of such a survivor or other unnecessary conditions unless required by law or funding source. 249 44 b. The Contractor’s procedures and oversight must demonstrate that staff do everything possible to avoid denying assistance or rejecting an individual or family for the reasons listed within section 2(a). c. The Contractor shall provide equal access in accordance with the 2012 and 2016 Equal Access Rules, meaning that any project funded by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) must ensure equal access for persons regardless of one’s sexual orientation or marital status, and in accordance with one’s gender identity. Adult households, regardless of marital status, should have equal access to the program. d. The Contractor shall have an expedited admissions process, to the greatest extent possible, including helping participants obtain documentation required by funding sources, as well as processes to admit participants regardless of the status of their eligibility documentation whenever possible. e. Intake and assessment procedures will be focused on the individual’s or family’s strengths, needs, and preferences. Programs should not require specific appointment times but have flexible intake schedules that ensure access to all households. Assessments are focused on identifying barriers to housing that can inform the basis of a housing plan as soon as a person is enrolled in the program. f. The Contractor shall actively participate in the Merced CoC’s Coordinated Entry process as a part of a streamlined community-wide system access triage. Referrals from Coordinated Entry must be rarely rejected, and only if there is a history of violence, the participant does not want to be in the program, there are legally valid grounds (such as restrictions regarding sex offender) or some other exceptional circumstance that is well documented. g. For programs that can no longer serve particular households, the Contractor shall utilize the Coordinated Entry process to ensure that those individuals and families have access to other housing and services as desired, and do not become disconnected from services and housing. Households that encounter exits under these circumstances, such as if they demonstrate violent or harassing behaviors, are to be described with the Contractor’s regulation adherent policies. 7. Service Targeting The Contractor shall not target services towards a specific sub-population or specific geographical area within the jurisdiction of the County of Merced without prior approval from the AE, unless otherwise identified by the grant or funding source. Services must be provided to all program eligible clients without regard to their age, gender, race, ethnicity, mental health, physical health, substance use, veteran status, income, citizenship, or location within the County of Merced. 250 45 8. Disruptions of Service The Contractor shall notify the AE as soon as the Contractor becomes aware of any disruptions in service. Noticing shall not exceed forty-eight (48) hours from the initial awareness of the disruption. The Contractor shall provide a statement in writing to include the reason, the duration, and solution to resolve the disruption. 9. Responsiveness of Communications The Contractor shall provide timely and effective communication with the AE throughout the term of this Agreement. The Contractor shall designate one or more qualified personnel to serve as the primary point(s) of contact and shall notify the AE of any changes to the designated contact(s) or contact information. The Contractor shall be available for communication during normal business hours, excluding recognized holidays. In the event of planned downtime or limited availability (e.g., holidays, system maintenance), the Contractor shall provide the AE with at least three (3) business days advance notice. If the Contractor fails to meet the responsiveness timeframes outlined above, the AE may escalate the issue to the Contractor’s designated escalation contact. The Contractor agrees to provide escalation contact details upon execution of this Agreement and to keep such information current throughout the term. The AE may monitor and evaluate the Contractor’s responsiveness as part of its contract monitoring process. 10. Program Capacity The Contractor shall maintain sufficient capacity, including staffing, infrastructure, and technical resources, to fully support their program operations for the duration of this Agreement and to avoid any disruptions of service. This includes ensuring that all necessary systems, personnel, and materials are available and properly managed to meet the performance requirements and timelines outlined in this agreement. The Contractor shall ensure that all staff have the necessary resources, training, and capacity to effectively perform the duties and responsibilities of the program. 11. Public Records Act Requests The Contractor shall direct individuals requesting records regarding the AE under the Public Records Act to submit their request to the Merced County Human Services Agency located at 2115 Wardrobe Ave, Merced, CA 95341 or mailed with attention to “Public Records Act Request” to P.O. Box 112, Merced, CA 95341-0112 or at the Merced County Counsel’s Office located at 2222 M St, Merced, CA 95430. 251 46 The Contractor shall immediately forward every Public Records Act request regarding the AE to collabapp@countyofmerced.com. The Contactor shall supply records requested by the AE for Public Record Act requests within forty-eight (48) hours. 12. Contract Monitoring The Contractor shall be monitored by the Contract Monitoring Team (CMT) comprising of AE staff to ensure grant funded projects and programs are implemented in accordance with relevant rules, regulations, and grant requirements set forth by this Agreement as well as the Agreement’s corresponding funding source(s). The Contractor agrees that the CMT or its designee shall have the right to review, obtain, and copy all records and supporting documentation pertaining to the performance of this Agreement. The Contractor shall provide the CMT or its designee with any relevant information requested. The Contractor agrees to permit the AE or its designee access to its premises, upon reasonable notice, during normal business hours for the purpose of interviewing employees who might reasonably have information related to such records and inspecting and copying such books, records, accounts, and other material that may be relevant to a matter under investigation for the purpose of determining compliance with the funding statues, Notice of Funding Opportunities (NOFO), Notice of Funding Availability (NOFA), and this agreement. The AE may request additional information as needed to meet other applicable audit or reporting requirements. The CMT reserves the right to monitor all work performed by the Contractor and subcontractors in relation to this Agreement at the Contractor’s expense at any point during the retention period of this Agreement. An onsite or virtual monitoring visit shall occur whenever determined necessary, but at least once a year at the discretion of the CMT and at the expense of the Contractor. At the CMT’s request and at the Contractor's expense, a financial audit shall be conducted by a certified public accountant. The CMT will rely primarily on information obtained from the records and reports furnished by the Contractor and subcontractors, as well as information from the onsite monitoring, audit reports, and information generated from the CMT’s financial and reporting systems, and the Homeless Management Information System (HMIS). Where applicable, the CMT may also consider relevant information pertaining to the Contractor’s performance gained from other sources, including client feedback, complaint determinations, and litigation. If the CMT determines preliminarily that the Contractor and/or subcontractors has not complied with a program requirement, the CMT will issue a notice of this 252 47 determination and an opportunity to demonstrate on the basis of substantial facts and data that the recipient has complied with the requirements. Responses are due no later than thirty (30) days from the issuance of the notice by the CMT. If the recipient fails to demonstrate to the CMT’s satisfaction that the activities were carried out in compliance with program requirements, the CMT may take one or more of the remedial actions or sanctions specified. Remedial actions or sanctions for failure to meet a program requirement will be designed to prevent a continuation of the deficiency, to mitigate to the extent possible its adverse effects or consequences and to prevent its recurrence. If the CMT determines that a Contractor or subcontractor is not complying with a program requirement or its agreement, in accordance with 24 CFR 578.107 the CMT may: 1. Prepare and follow a schedule of actions for carrying out activities and projects affected by the noncompliance, including schedules, timetables, and milestones necessary to implement the affected activities and projects; 2. Establish and follow a management plan that assigns responsibilities for carrying out the remedial actions; 3. Cancel or revise activities or projects likely to be affected by the noncompliance, before expending grant funds; 4. Reprogram grant funds that have not yet been expended from affected activities or projects to other eligible activities or projects: 5. Suspend disbursements of grant funds for some or all activities or projects; 6. Reduce or terminate the remaining funding of a Contractor and either reallocate those funds to other Contractors or return the funds to the funding agency; 7. Condition the award of future agreements; or 8. Other legally available remedies. 13. Reporting Requirements The Contractor shall provide monthly grantee reports, by request, to the Collaborative Applicant at collabapp@countyofmerced.com to the AE no later than 15th day of the month following the date of service delivery. Reports shall be per project and shall include, but are not limited to, the following: 1. Clients Served – Unduplicated; 2. Clients Served – Duplicated; 3. Clients on Waiting List; 4. Client Program Exit Outcomes; 5. Service Referrals; 6. Progress Towards the Completion of Mutually Agreed Upon Goals; 7. Disaggregated HMIS Racial and Ethnic Client Data; 8. HMIS Gender Data; 9. Total Number of Beds/Units; 253 48 10. Number of Vacant Beds/Units; 11. Instances of the Duplication of Benefits 12. Program Feedback Analysis; 13. Expenditures for Reporting Period; 14. Grant Expenditures to Date; and 15. Remaining Funding Balance. The Contractor shall provide any and all program or project data required to complete any reporting required by the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD), HUD, the U.S. Department of the Treasury, the Business, Consumer Services and Housing Agency (BCSH), the Department of Health Care Services (DHCS), and other relevant agencies. 14. Recordkeeping and Retention The Contractor shall maintain compliance with the recordkeeping requirements of 24 CFR 576.500 and 24 CFR 578.103. The Contractor agrees to retain all records for a minimum of five (5) years following the termination of this agreement. The Contractor shall maintain the following records for each client and make these records available to the AE upon request. Document Type Street Outreach Emergency Shelter Homelessness Prevention Rapid Re-Housing Area Median Income Verification  Assessments / Reassessments     Case Notes     Certification of Homelessness    Certification of Imminent Risk / At Risk  Client Risk Factors     Client Vulnerability Factors     Duplication of Benefits Analysis   Eviction Notices   Fair Market Rent Certification   Grievances, Appeals, and Incidents     Housing Habitability Inspection   Housing Stability Plan    Ineligibility Determination     Intake/Enrollment Packet     Landlord W-9   Lead Based Paint Screening   Release of Information (HMIS)     Release of Information (Program)     Rent Amount Change Notices   Rent Reasonableness Analysis   254 49 Document Type Street Outreach Emergency Shelter Homelessness Prevention Rapid Re-Housing Rental Agreement (Lease)   Rental Assistance Agreement   Utility Statements   VAWA Lease Addendum   Verification of Income   Verification of Service Payments     15. Policies and Procedures The Contractor shall develop, implement, and maintain written policies and procedures that fully detail and provide sufficient information about the operations for all programs and projects. These policies and procedures shall be detailed enough that a person who is not familiar with the project could reasonably reconstruct the project from these documents. These policies and procedures must comply with any and all federal, state, and local laws, statues, and regulations. Additionally, they must be in alignment and comply with Written Standards, Policies, and Procedures as provided by the Merced CoC located on the Merced CoC website:  The Contractor shall develop policies and procedure to include, but is not limited to, the following: a. Anti-Discrimination, Harassment, and Retaliation b. Client Assessment/Eligibility – Intake Process c. Codes of Conduct d. Confidentiality (Personal Identification Information) e. Conflicts of Interest f. Coordinated Entry System (CES) g. Drug-Free Policy Statement h. Duplication of Benefits i. Emergency Shelter j. Grievances and Appeals k. Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) l. Homelessness Prevention m. Rapid Re-Housing n. Release of Information o. Women Against Women Act (VAWA) – Emergency Transfer Plan (ETP) 16. Program Feedback The Contractor shall implement and maintain a systematic process to gather feedback from program participants regarding their satisfaction with services provided. This feedback shall be collected at regular intervals, at a minimum of bi-annually, through methods such as surveys, interviews, focus groups, or other suitable mechanisms approved by the AE. The feedback should assess the overall 255 50 quality of care, responsiveness of staff, and the effectiveness of services provided. The Contractor shall establish a regular process for collecting feedback from staff members regarding their satisfaction with the program's operations, management, and resources. This feedback shall be gathered through anonymous surveys, staff meetings, or other methods that ensure confidentiality and encourage honest input. Feedback shall be collected at least annually and should address staff workload, working conditions, and support systems available to them. The Contractor shall analyze the collected feedback from both clients and staff to identify trends, concerns, and areas for improvement. A summary of this analysis, along with a corrective action plan, shall be submitted to the AE quarterly as part of the program's performance report or grantee reporting. The Contractor shall outline any steps taken to address feedback, improve client and staff satisfaction, and enhance program effectiveness. The Contractor shall demonstrate responsiveness to feedback by making program adjustments as necessary to improve service delivery. This may include revising program processes, increasing staff training, or modifying services based on the feedback received. The Contract shall be expected to take concrete actions in response to feedback within ninety (90) days of receiving it. The Contractor shall ensure that all feedback, whether from clients or staff, is treated with confidentiality and that no retaliation occurs against individuals who provide feedback. The provider must have a clear policy in place to protect participants and staff members from retaliation in any form. 17. Complaint, Grievance, and Incident Reporting The Contractor shall notify the AE of any and all client-filed complaints, grievances, or incident reports within forty-eight (48) hours of receipt. The Contractor shall furnish a running log of all events and all supporting documentation to the AE on a monthly basis. The AE does not hereby assume responsibility for such grievances or incident reports by being provided notice and documentation of such events. 18. Homeless Management Information System (HMIS) 24 CFR 578.7(b) tasks CoC’s with designating and operating a Homeless Management Information System (HMIS). Additionally, 24 CFR 578.7(b)(4) requires consistent participation of recipients and subrecipients in HMIS. To maintain compliance under these regulations, the Contractor shall utilize the Merced CoC approved assessment tool to conduct initial assessments on individuals or families seeking homeless assistance services and enter all assessment information into HMIS. 256 51 The Contractor shall utilize and integrate the Merced City and County Continuum of Care (Merced CoC) HMIS into program processes and operations. Program processes and operations shall comply with the Merced CoC HMIS Policy and Procedures. The Contractor is required to utilize HMIS to document client data, case management notes, and offered/provided services to all individuals and families experiencing homelessness. Entered data shall comply with HUD’s HMIS Data Standards and shall be monitored by the Contractor for quality and accuracy. The Contractor shall enter all client level and service level data into HMIS in a timely manner so as to not impede the reporting, prioritization, data analysis, or informed decision-making process. The Contractor shall ensure all information entered into the HMIS is accurate, up-to-date, and complete. This includes, but is not limited to, client demographics, service delivery data, case notes, assessments, referrals, housing status, and any other relevant information required by the AE or HMIS Lead. The Contractor shall ensure all relevant staff are trained on HMIS data entry procedures and best practices. The Contractor shall maintain internal procedures to review and verify data accuracy on a regular basis. The Contractor shall correct any discrepancies, inaccuracies, or omissions in the data promptly and document such corrections. The Contractor shall submit data within the required timeframes as established by the AE. The Contractor agrees to provide the AE access to HMIS data collected and entered by the Contractor into HMIS. Upon request, the Contractor shall participate in any statewide initiative including but not limited to, a statewide data integration environment. 19. Coordinated Entry System (CES) 24 CFR 578.7(a)(8) requires CoCs establish and operate either a centralized or coordinated assessment system that provides an initial, comprehensive assessment of the needs of individuals and families for housing and services. Additional requirements were also supplied with HUD Notice CPD-17-01. Towards this end, the Contractor shall actively participate in the Coordinated Entry System (CES). The Merced CoC identified assessment tool will be utilized to determine priority listing for individuals or families seeking homeless assistance services. The CES priority list will be pulled from the assessment data entered into HMIS and used to provide services needs in a priority order to homeless or at risk of homelessness individuals and families requesting assistance. The Contractor shall utilize and integrate the Merced City and County Continuum of Care (Merced CoC) Coordinated Entry System (CES) into program processes and operations. Program processes and operations shall comply with the Merced CoC CES Policy and Procedures. 257 52 The Contractor shall utilize the Merced CoC designated assessment tool. The Contractor shall make referrals to and receive referrals from the CES. This includes presenting individual cases, as applicable, at the CES meetings to determine appropriate service provider(s) referral(s). The Contractor shall collaborate with community partners, service providers, and local governmental agencies to case manage and provide unduplicated services. The Contractor shall attend and actively participate in the CES meetings as scheduled by the CES Lead. These meetings are conducted to discuss client needs and identify resources to help house and/or stabilize the individual. 20. CoC Meetings The Contractor shall attend and participate in the monthly Merced City and County Continuum of Care (CoC) meetings which occur on the first Thursday of each month. The Contractor shall maintain a good standing as a CoC General Member throughout the duration of this agreement. General Member requirements are detailed within the Merced CoC Governance Charter available on the Merced CoC website. 21. Annual Point-in-Time Count As required by HUD, CoC’s must conduct a “one-night, point-in-time” homeless count every other year during the last ten (10) days of January. The Merced CoC has opted to conduct this count annually. The Contractor may provide support for and be engaged in the Merced CoC annual Point-in-Time count. 22. Annual Housing Inventory Count As required by HUD, CoC’s must conduct a point-in-time inventory of programs that provide beds and units dedicated to serve people experiencing homelessness. The five program types included are Emergency Shelter, Transitional Housing, Rapid Re-Housing, Safe Haven, and Permanent Supportive Housing. The Contractor shall provide support for and be engaged in the data gathering, analysis, and submission of the Merced CoC Housing Inventory Count. 23. Project and Funding Sustainability When available and feasible, the Contractor shall make reasonable efforts to braid new and existing funding sources to sustain the project without duplicating any of the funding or services. Funding availability varies significantly from year to year. In the absence of available resources, the Contractor is highly encouraged to plan for obtaining the funding necessary for sustaining their project(s) during and beyond the term of this Agreement without supplanting funds. Leveraging available 258 53 funding sources is key to ensuring there isn’t a disruption of services to our clients and community members. 24. Inventory Management The Contractor shall establish controls to ensure adequate safeguards to prevent loss, damage, or theft to property, including equipment purchased with Agreement funds. If Contractor should no longer provide services under this Agreement, the equipment and property shall be returned to the AE. The Contractor shall be responsible for managing and tracking all supplies and equipment purchased with program funding. Fixed assets, IT equipment, and item purchases over $1,000.00 must be tagged and tracked. These items shall be inventoried by the Contractor at least annually and made available for review at the request of the AE. Items must be disposed of or surplus in compliance with terms and conditions of the funding sources used to purchase the item with prior notice and approval from the AE. All property including computer software, hardware, equipment, furniture, motorized items, and fixed assets purchased with AE funds must be returned to the AE following the termination of this Agreement. Thirty (30) days prior to the termination of this Agreement, all Contractor owned property shall be segregated from AE owned property. An inventory shall be conducted by Contractor and the AE to verify the proper separation and relinquishment of AE owned assets, equipment, supplies, and technical data/documentation. 25. Contractor’s Application for Funds The Contractor has applied through a Request for Proposal (RFP) submission for funding to provide the services outlined within this agreement. Contractor is entering into this Agreement on the basis of, and in substantial reliance upon, Contractor’s facts, information, assertions and representations contained within that application, and in any subsequent modifications or additions thereto. The Contractor warrants that all information, facts, assertions, and representations contained in the application and approved modifications and additions thereto are true, correct, and complete to the best of the Contractor’s knowledge. In the event that any part of the application and any approved modification and addition thereto is untrue, incorrect, incomplete, or misleading in such a manner that would substantially affect the approval, disbursement, or monitoring of the funding and the grants or activities governed by this agreement, then the AE may declare a breach hereof and take such action or pursue such remedies as are provided for breach hereof. 259 260

# behavior  basics 

Why do children misbehave? The simple answer comes down to consequences.  aL ison Betz , assis-tant professor of psychology, explains how a few simple ground rules can make a big difference in changing a child’s behavior. 

Ru LE  1: R EI nFORCE  (REWARD ) GOOD  bEHAVIOR  … qu ICKLY  AnD

OFTE n. 

When your child is rewarded for a particular behavior, that behavior is strengthened and more likely to occur again. This means you can’t take good behavior for granted. Be sure you pay atten-tion to the good behaviors and reinforce the way you want your child to behave. Do this frequently and immediately after good behaviors occur. 

Ru LE  2: T RY  nOT  TO  ACCIDE nTAL LY  REWARD  bAD  bEHAVIOR .

When poor behavior is reinforced, it too is strengthened and more likely to occur in the future. Beware of accidentally rewarding inappropriate behavior by “giving in” or paying attention to the behavior when all your child wants is your attention. When you “give in” to a tantrum—even in an effort to avoid a scene in public, it teaches children that such behavior will get them what they want. 

Ru LE  3: T EACH  MORE  APPROPRIATE  bEHAVIORS  THAT  CA n REPLACE 

THE  MILD  InAPPROPRIATE  bEHAVIORS .

When children act out in a mild way, like whin-ing, saying “no” or not listening, try to teach them a better way to get what they want. Introduce these teaching opportunities, however, only with the mild behaviors and not the intensely inappropriate behaviors. A child is probably not listening when he or she is engaging in a tantrum, so wait for the right time to teach the replacement behaviors. Often times, these rules are easier said than done. The key is to monitor your behavior as much as you do your child’s.

# q. W HY  EnCO uRAGE  YO un G PEOPLE  TO  ST uDY  MATH ?In modern societies, mathematics is an important part of everyday life. To function well in a technologically advanced society, every person should be familiar with multiple aspects of the mathematical sciences. 

Although the mathematical sciences are pervasive, they are often invoked without an explicit awareness of their presence. For example, in the everyday operation of making a cell phone call, the mathemati-cal sciences are essential in every step. We enter numbers in the deci-mal system, which are converted into sequences of bits (zeros and ones). Next comes conversion to an electromagnetic signal. After an available receiver is located, the signal is transmitted and converted into the sound of our voice. Wireless technology uses techniques called “error correcting codes,” “linear and nonlinear filtering,” “hypothesis testing,” “spatial multi-plexing” and “statistical waveform or parameter estimation.” These are built on tools of the mathematical sciences such as matrix analysis, linear algebra, algebra, random matrices and graphical models 1.Many other technological advances such as  cD and D vD play-ers, Internet, Google, social network engines (Facebook, Twitter, etc.), computer games, pacemakers (for hearts), brain pacemakers (for Parkinson’s disease patients), medical imaging devices (M rI,  cT, Pet 

scan) and electric toothbrushes are based on mathematical ideas. In a nutshell, mathematics is the building block of scientific and technological inventions. Decades from now, when young kids are at the peak of their career, if they don’t know these building blocks, they will feel the deficiency no matter what their job requires.

Fresh on the heels of a Florida Tech management degree and a Notre Dame MBA, he had his pick of positions in banking, consulting or industry. “What I like about Ford is under one umbrella, one major multinational company, you could—and I did—have opportunities to work in many different areas,” he says. He climbed the ladder of corporate finance, while being exposed to product development and engineering, manu-facturing, banking, mergers and acqui-sitions, recruiting and international business. In fact, the highlight of his tenure at Ford was 11 years spent overseas as the chief financial officer for the company’s divisions in Venezuela, Brazil, Taiwan and South Africa—the operations at each destination growing progressively larger in scope. “I was fortunate in that the jobs I had in the States tended to have a broad perspective on things, but you still didn’t have input and effect on the entire business,” he says. In his international assignments, he enjoyed that macro-level involvement. “You were controlling and working with the operating teams in each loca-tion to effectively make all the decisions and make money for the company,” he says. “The 11 years I spent overseas were the best part of my career.” The experiences were rewarding both professionally and personally. Phebus and his wife Deborah enjoyed extensive travel and culinary adventures and developed broad cross-cultural awareness. His contributions to his alma mater parallel those of his career—taking a leadership role with both the Florida Tech Alumni Association board of directors and later the university’s board of trustees to support and guide the university. In 1995 at the invitation of then-board president CHar Lie  mCsH ane 

’75, a friend from his campus days, Phebus joined the FTAA board of directors. At the time, the FTAA was still in its infancy and was struggling to get alumni reconnected with the univer-sity. One of Phebus’ first tasks as a board member was organizing a market research study to survey alumni on what they wanted from their alumni association. “Based on the responses we received, we tried to structure programs differently and structure the organiza-tion differently so that we could be more responsive to people’s needs,” he says. With the growth and progress of the alumni association and the univer-sity as a whole, he feels those early efforts were a success. Leveraging his time in Taiwan, he also played an active role in secur-ing funding for the refurbishment of the Chao Tsu-Yu Chinese Clock that stands in front of the Keuper Building. Taiwanese officials presented the clock to the university in 1981 in recognition of Florida Tech’s leadership in grant-ing graduate fellowships to Chinese students in the 1970s and 1980s. “It’s really quite an interesting clock with an interesting history,” Phebus says. “I’m glad to see that it’s still in good working order.” His FTAA board service continued through 2003, with a stint as president in 1996–1997. Today, he is a member of the board of trustees, serving on the audit committee, the finance committee and the investment committee. Phebus’ leadership and loyalty— both in his career and in his service to the university—exemplify the ideals of the Jerome P. Keuper Distinguished Alumnus award and make him a fitting recipient for this year’s honor.

Page 5 The Hinsdalean Thursday, June 27, 2024 Hinsdale, Illinois Volume XVIII, Issue 41 $1 on Newsstands - 40 Pages • • • After throwing out the first pitch for the Clarendon Hills Softball Queen of the Hills tournament, Hinsdale’s Alexander Brown took over the microphone to shout, “Play ball!” The 10U round robin tournament was hosted by the Lady Red Devils June 9. Proceeds from the event went to benefit the Make-A-Wish Illinois organization. Alexander is currently undergoing treatment for a brain tumor and will be starting kindergarten at The Lane School this fall. He is also looking forward to his Make-A-Wish Disney cruise this fall. Please turn to Page 26 for more pictures. To learn more about Alexander’s story visit www.alexanderstrong.org. SPARKLING WATER The Hinsdalean • June 27 2024 • Page 3 news MAP test scores are good news for D181 By Pamela Lannom plannom@thehinsdalean.com Spring MAP test scores show Community Consolidated Elementary District 181 students are continuing to outperform their peers, with most showing a higher than expected level of growth.
Thirty-four percent of students scored in the 90-99th percentile on the Measurement of Academic Progress in reading, with almost 60 percent scoring in the top decile in math, Kristin Reingruber told board members at their June 17 meeting. Seventy-two percent scored in the top three decile bands (70-79, 80-89 and 90-99) in reading and 83 per-cent did so in math.
Reingruber, the district’s direc-tor of assessment, instruction and evaluation, shared slides showing student’s performance in the var-ious decile bands. No bell curves were to be seen. “We do not see the typical curve that you do see across other dis-tricts,” she said. “I had to make the graph smaller and slide it over a little bit.” All but three grades at all nine schools exceeded the 50 percent growth target in reading.
“Across the board we are signifi-cantly above or right at that num-ber,” Reingruber said. “These are really exciting numbers to see.” Walker first-graders showed the highest percentage growth at 84.3. Madison third-graders, Monroe fifth-graders and Hinsdale Middle School sixth-graders fell below the 50 percent benchmark, showing 45.3 to 46.5 percent growth.
In math, all but two grades saw more than 50 percent growth. Walker first-graders again showed the most at 96.1 percent, with 16 grades showing growth of 80 per-cent or more. Madison fifth-grad-ers and HMS sixth-graders showed 49.2 and 46.9 percent growth, respectively. Board member Grace Shin noted that the district purchased a new math curriculum two years ago.
“I think we’re seeing the fruits of those results right now,” Shin said.
Principals presented their school improvement plans to academic success committee members earli-er in the day June 17.
“Our teams are going to contin-ue to reflect on both the academic and the social-emotional strategies. Their goal is to be intentional to meet the needs of all their learn-ers,” Reingruber said.
Board member Margie Kleber offered her congratulations to the department of learning.
“This is amazing. Every year I’m blown away,” she said.
“I love the fact that we continue to push that bar higher and high-er,” Superintendent Hector Garcia commented. “What a great way to end the year.” Sunday drivers Fuelfed hosted another classic car event June 9 on Chicago Avenue at Burlington Park. Featuring classic European cars from 1995 or earlier, the theme for the morning was “Women Drivers & Kids Sticker Day.” Jack Herbert led dad Chris around the street viewing the cars. Tom Darham was quick to point out he was showcasing his wife Daria’s 1967 Jaguar E-Type 4.2 XKE. The next Fuelfed event is scheduled for Aug. 4 and will feature Italian classics. ................................................................... 38 once upon a time The Hinsdalean • June 27 2024 • Page 5 Monday market starts the week off right From berries to baked goods, stands offer delicious treats to tempt the summer palate By Sandy Illian Bosch news@thehinsdalean.com The weekly farmer’s market on Chicago Avenue between Garfield and Washington streets has been part of Hinsdale for 48 years, and Rob Pondelick’s family has been present for every one of them. Pondelick is the fifth-gen-eration owner of Theis Farm Market in Maple Park, one of several farm-based busi-nesses in Pondelick’s family and one of two produce-pro-ducing farms to participate in the Monday market offered by the Hinsdale Chamber of Commerce. “For a Monday morning, it’s not too bad,” Pondelick said of the crowd seeking his stand’s fresh fruits and vegetables. Speaking from years of expe-rience, Pondelick expects the crowds to get even bigger after the Fourth of July, when the variety of produce expands. “That’s when it really gets poppin,’ ” he said. Pondelick rises at about 3 a.m. each Monday to pre-pare for the hour-long trip to Hinsdale. It’s one of five mar-kets on his weekly schedule.
While Pondelick is travel-ing east, the folks from Kugel Farms of Berrien Springs, Mich., are making their way around Lake Michigan in time for the market’s 7 a.m. start. The Kugel Farms stand is a favorite on Laila Alamuddin’s weekly outing to the Hinsdale market. She said she’s been visiting the market since 2011 to stock up on homegrown, fresh food. That includes eggs and meat from Farmer Nick’s. “We love it,” she said. On this particular Monday, Alamuddin stocked up on fresh berries for smoothies and ingredients for a gathering she had planned for later in the week. While Alamuddin comes to the market for healthy food she can make herself, ven-dor Maple & Yam offers up prepared dishes made with those same simple, healthy ingredients. Married couple Bob Lewandowski and Diana Luna of Clarendon Hills began the business just seven months ago, naming it after one of their most popular cre-ations — yams seasoned with real Vermont maple syrup. It, along with barbecue meat-balls, pot roast sliders and breakfast sandwiches made with organic eggs, is hot and ready to go every Monday. Lewandowski said he spends about eight hours a day cooking the food he sells at area markets each week. He uses ingredients like grass-fed beef, organic eggs, fresh vege-tables and real butter. “We want to stay true to the ‘farm-to-table,’ ” and support local farmers, Luna said. Located next to Burlington Park, the market offers plenty of room for people to gather for a chat or relax with a treat from one of the market’s nine food trucks. That’s where 10-year-old Sloan Allegretti chose to enjoy her acai bowl from Bao Acai.
“There’s always a new stand,” said Sloan, who called her first acai bowl “awesome.” Sloan’s mother, Barbie, said the market is a great way to spend a summer morning with her children. “It’s a nice family outing,” she said, and a chance for her daughters to try new foods and fresh, seasonal produce. Sloan said she’s looking forward to enjoying the peaches, plums and nectarines she remembers from last year’s offerings. Among the market’s nearly 30 vendors are bakeries with freshly made treats and local businesses selling products from home improvements to houseplants. New to the market this summer is Hestia Grinds, a brother-sister team bringing signature-blend cof-fees to the market. Samuel and Alex Cardenas said they work with family farms all over the world to create their brand’s unique flavors. Shoppers can grab a cup of cold or hot brew, a bag of whole or ground beans or even a growler or cans of coffee to go. The market continues every Monday from 7 a.m. to 1 p.m. through Oct. 14. Police enforcement to increase before July 4 The Hinsdale Police Department has is stepping up Fourth of July traffic enforce-ment with a focus on impaired and unbuckled driver through the early-morning hours of July 8.
“It’s a straightforward mes-sage: If you’re behind the wheel, stay sober. Don’t drink, use marijuana, or consume any other impairing substanc-es before or when driving,” said Deputy Chief Thomas Lillie. Follow these tips to help ensure a happy and safe hol-iday: • Designate a sober driver and give them your keys before you go out.
• Don’t let friends or fami-ly members drive under the influence.
• If you are drunk or impaired by marijuana or other drugs, call a taxi, take mass transit, use your favor-ite ride-sharing app or call a sober friend or family member to get you home safely.
• Promptly report drunken drivers to law enforcement by pulling over and dialing 911.
• Make sure everyone in the vehicle wears their seat belt. It’s not only the law, but also your best defense against an impaired driver.
The statewide “Drive Sober or Get Pulled Over,” “Drive High Get a DUI” and “Click It or Ticket” programs are made possible by federal highway safety funds administered by the Illinois Department of Transportation. The enforce-ment period runs concurrent-ly with IDOT’s media cam-paign, reminding motorists that “It’s Not a Game” to drive impaired.

Briones Simpson 60 SECONDS The Hinsdalean • June 27 2024 • Page 9 Shortly after moving to Hinsdale from Chicago in 2021, Hinsdale’s Alex LaRoia signed up for a baby music class hoping to enrich the bond with her child.
She had no idea the extent to which her personal con-nections also would flourish.
“I met some girls who were in (Hinsdale Junior Woman’s Club), and that opened up the floodgates to my entryway to the club,” LaRoia said. Leadership posts in Juniors followed, first as new mem-ber chair and currently as one of the philanthropy co-chairs of the community service-ori-ented group, leveraging her background in social work. “We oversee the entire grant-making process and our service projects,” said LaRoia, who is able to lean into her social work back-ground. “It felt like a natural fit to take on this role.” She’s been busy recent-ly helping coordinate the “Sunsets in Santorini”-themed summer party benefit on July 20 (see Page 18 for details). All of the ticket pro-ceeds will be used to support worthy agencies, she said. Miss Illinois will even make an appearance to advocate for Bernie’s Book Bank, promoing literacy among under-resourced youth, and guests are invited to bring a children’s book to donate.
“It’s a nice nod to what the club is about: community and philanthropy,” LaRoia said.
Organizers have also planned an homage to mark Juniors’ 75th year, with arti-facts including cookbooks early members compiled as a fundraiser.
“It’s a real way to honor the legacy of the club and also to light the path to where we’re going in the future,” she said. “The reason why it started in 1949 was not only to enrich the lives of the community but to give back.” The gatherings the group holds may seem social in nature, LaRoia acknowl-edged, but they are parties with a purpose. “We are raising a lot of money to give away to peo-ple,” she said. “Last year we raised over $300,000 and gave it to 21 different organizations and (awarded) four different scholarships.” LaRoia, who works for a family-owned natural stone firm, recounted the challenge of securing a home during the crazy market during the pandemic.
“We had to write a letter and put our family photo in the letter,” she recounted. “It was like, ‘Pick me!’ ” LaRoia and her family like to travel when time permits, and she looks forward to walking her oldest to school in the fall when he starts kin-dergarten.
“I feel very blessed to be here,” she said. “Hinsdale feels very idyllic. We’re just trying to give our kids that good old-fashioned child-hood.” And it’s worked out well for the parents, too. “We’ve met so many people through the club, so many like-minded people and young families,” LaRoia said. “Now I know so many more people at the grocery store and in town because of the club. It’s been a critical part of my transition from the city.” Helping carry on the tra-dition of Hinsdale Junior Woman’s Club has been an unexpected reward to mak-ing the village their home.
“It’s definitely a point of pride being in it, because the work that we do is outstand-ing,” she said.
